messages.content:
Rate the following clinical vignette:

Leilani traces the clean, confident line of a support beam on the blueprint before her, but the image wavers. For nearly thirty years, her gift has been an almost preternatural ability to see structure, to understand how foundations bear weight, and to envision safe, enduring spaces from nothing but ink and paper. Now, her own foundation feels like it's built on sand.

It has been two years since the phone call that fractured her world. It was 3:17 AM. She remembers the exact time because she had been awake, reviewing schematics for a coastal community center, a project meant to withstand a category four hurricane. The detached, professional voice of the emergency room doctor offered no such resilience. There had been an accident. Her son, Manu, had been hit by a drunk driver while riding his scooter home from his restaurant job.

The hours that followed are a collection of sensory shards: the searing fluorescent lights of the hospital hallway, the sterile smell that failed to mask the scent of fear, the rhythmic, terrifying beep of the machines tethered to her son. Manu was unrecognizable, a landscape of tubes, bandages, and swollen flesh. She, the architect who designed homes to shelter families, could do nothing to shelter her own child from this. She remembers placing her hand on his uninjured foot, the only part of him that felt familiar, and realizing she had never felt so powerless.

Manu survived. The doctors called it a miracle. But the Manu who came home after months of surgeries and rehabilitation was a different man. The easy laugh was gone, replaced by a quiet, pained frustration. His body, once so strong and fluid, was now a map of his trauma, and he walked with a permanent limp.

Leilani's life, once a well-designed structure, began to show its own fault lines. She threw herself back into her work, believing the familiar logic of load-bearing walls and spatial harmony could save her. But the trauma followed her there. The screech of a delivery truck's brakes outside her office sends the metallic taste of panic to her mouth and the ghostly smell of the ICU to her nostrils. She finds herself staring at a blueprint for minutes on end, the lines blurring, her mind replaying the image of Manu's broken body on the hospital bed.

Sleep offers no escape. She is plagued by nightmares of screeching tires and shattering glass, waking up with her heart hammering against her ribs, drenched in sweat. During the day, a relentless, quiet dread hums beneath the surface of everything. She feels a profound detachment from her colleagues, their conversations about deadlines and material costs sounding like a language from a world she no longer inhabits. She won awards for designing spaces that foster community, yet she actively avoids friends and family, tired of the pity in their eyes and the effort of pretending she is okay. She and her husband divorced last year; he said it was like living with a ghost. He wasn't wrong.

She takes a twenty-minute detour on her way to work every morning to avoid the intersection where Manu was hit. She can no longer listen to the radio in the car, terrified of a news report about another accident. A late-night phone call sends a jolt of pure terror through her system. The world, which she once navigated with confidence, now feels fundamentally unsafe, a place where catastrophe can strike at any moment, without reason or warning.

Leilani looks down at the plans on her desk. It is a beautiful design, a library with soaring ceilings and vast windows, a space meant to be a sanctuary. But all she can see are the vulnerabilities, the points of failure, the million ways it could all come crashing down. She, who spent a lifetime building things to last, now lives with the unshakable certainty that nothing is permanent and nothing is safe.

These sentences explicitly describe avoidance of an external reminder (the intersection) and avoidance of potential trauma-related content (news about accidents), clearly demonstrating Criterion C.
